Leery

LEER-ee -- of uncertain origin, possibly related to an old dialect word 'leer' meaning to look sideways or askance. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Leery is cautious and suspicious of someone or something, usually because of past experience.

Investors grew leery of the startup's rosy sales projections once its first two products quietly failed.

Worked Example

Having been bitten twice by the same stray dog, the mail carrier grew leery of that particular house and always checked the yard before approaching.

That lingering wariness, built up from a specific bad experience, is exactly what it means to be leery of something.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distrustful: unwilling to trust someone or something

skeptical: having doubts about whether something is true or reliable

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

confident: feeling sure and free of doubt

credulous: too willing to believe things without enough evidence

Where it sits · how much convincing they need — distrustful → leery → skeptical

distrustful vs. leery: Distrustful is milder than leery: a distrustful dog simply doesn't trust the vet's office, while a leery one stays actively on guard, flinching at every reach toward the exam table.

skeptical vs. leery: Reporters stayed skeptical of the company's numbers until an outside audit confirmed them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Leery's origin is genuinely uncertain -- it may come from an old dialect verb 'leer,' meaning to glance sideways or watchfully. Since the root doesn't cleanly extend into other common English words, leery is best learned as its own standalone term for cautious suspicion.

Use the root in a new word: leer

Use the root in a new word: leer: He gave the stranger a wary leer before deciding it was safe to answer the door.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Leery describes a mental state of wariness or suspicion -- it's almost always followed by 'of,' as in leery of a deal, a stranger, or a promise. Contrast this with gingerly, taught later in this unit, which describes careful physical movement rather than a feeling of suspicion.
